Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Depending on the application, we may define: Number of PCB layers Core and prepreg materials Copper thickness Dielectric thickness Controlled impedance requirements Power and ground reference planes Minimum trace width and spacing Via structures and drill sizes Manufacturing constraints For high-speed designs, impedance-controlled traces and their reference planes are considered from the beginning rather than being treated as an afterthought. The design rules are then configured in the EDA software to ensure that the layout remains consistent with both the electrical requirements and the PCB manufacturer's manufacturing capabilities. Step 3 – Component Placement Component placement is one of the most important stages of PCB layout because it establishes the physical structure of the entire board. The placement strategy typically starts with components whose locations are constrained by the mechanical design, such as: Connectors Switches and buttons Mounting holes Displays Mechanical interfaces Heat sinks and other thermal components Core components such as MCUs, CPUs, FPGAs, memory devices, power ICs, and communication ICs are then positioned according to signal flow, functional relationships, and electrical requirements. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. During placement, we consider several factors simultaneously: Signal Integrity High-speed interfaces and sensitive signals require appropriate component relationships and short, well-controlled routing paths. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Manufacturability Component spacing, assembly orientation, soldering requirements, and accessibility for inspection and rework are also considered. A well-planned placement makes subsequent routing more efficient while improving the overall reliability and manufacturability of the PCB. Step 4 – PCB Routing Once the component placement is finalized, the next stage is PCB routing. Routing is not simply about finding a path between two pads. The routing strategy must consider electrical performance, signal integrity, power distribution, EMI/EMC, and manufacturing constraints. Depending on the design, routing priorities may include: High-Speed and Critical Signals High-speed interfaces such as USB, DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS, and other differential interfaces may require: Controlled impedance Differential-pair routing Length matching Skew control Appropriate reference planes Minimized discontinuities Careful via transitions Critical signals are routed according to their electrical requirements rather than simply following the shortest available path. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Design Rule Check (DRC) Automated DRC is performed to identify potential violations such as: Clearance violations Trace width violations Unconnected nets Via and drill violations Component spacing issues Copper-to-board-edge violations Other manufacturer-specific rule violations Engineer Review Beyond automated DRC, the layout is also reviewed from an engineering perspective. Depending on the project, this may include checking: Signal integrity Power integrity Thermal performance EMI/EMC considerations High-speed routing Manufacturing constraints Assembly requirements Mechanical compatibility Automated checks can identify rule violations, but they cannot replace engineering judgment. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. For PCB assembly projects, the BOM and pick-and-place files provide the component and placement information required for SMT assembly. Before release, the output files are checked to ensure that the generated manufacturing data is consistent with the approved PCB design. Step 8 – DFM and PCB Manufacturing The final stage is transferring the verified manufacturing data into production. Before fabrication, the manufacturing data can be evaluated against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities through Design for Manufacturability (DFM) checks. Typical DFM considerations include: Minimum trace width and spacing Minimum drill size Copper-to-edge clearance Annular ring requirements Solder mask clearance Via structures Board thickness Copper thickness Surface finish Manufacturing tolerances Manufacturing requirements are considered from the very beginning of PCBWay's PCB layout process, helping minimize production issues and unnecessary manufacturing delays. What’s more, upon completion of the PCB Layout order, free technical support and a permanent 5% discount on PCBA production will be provided. Why Professional PCB Layout Matters PCB layout has a direct impact on the performance and manufacturability of an electronic product. A professional PCB layout should consider the entire product development process—not just whether all components are electrically connected. Depending on the application, the layout may need to address: Signal Integrity (SI) Power Integrity (PI) EMI/EMC Thermal Management High-Speed Design Design for Manufacturability (DFM) Design for Assembly (DFA) Mechanical Integration Reliability and Serviceability The earlier these factors are considered, the fewer problems are likely to appear during prototype validation and mass production. At PCBWay, our PCB design engineers work with customers throughout the layout process, helping transform circuit concepts and schematics into manufacturable, reliable, and production-ready PCB designs. If you are looking for professional PCB layout or PCB design services, feel free to contact us or submit PCB Layout requirement here. Our engineering team can help evaluate your design and develop a PCB layout optimized for both performance and manufacturing. PCB Layout Examples: From high-speed and RF to HDI, BGA, and rigid-flex designs, we handle a wide range of complex PCB layout requirements. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. During placement, we consider several factors simultaneously: Signal Integrity High-speed interfaces and sensitive signals require appropriate component relationships and short, well-controlled routing paths. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Manufacturability Component spacing, assembly orientation, soldering requirements, and accessibility for inspection and rework are also considered. A well-planned placement makes subsequent routing more efficient while improving the overall reliability and manufacturability of the PCB. Step 4 – PCB Routing Once the component placement is finalized, the next stage is PCB routing. Routing is not simply about finding a path between two pads. The routing strategy must consider electrical performance, signal integrity, power distribution, EMI/EMC, and manufacturing constraints. Depending on the design, routing priorities may include: High-Speed and Critical Signals High-speed interfaces such as USB, DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS, and other differential interfaces may require: Controlled impedance Differential-pair routing Length matching Skew control Appropriate reference planes Minimized discontinuities Careful via transitions Critical signals are routed according to their electrical requirements rather than simply following the shortest available path. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Design Rule Check (DRC) Automated DRC is performed to identify potential violations such as: Clearance violations Trace width violations Unconnected nets Via and drill violations Component spacing issues Copper-to-board-edge violations Other manufacturer-specific rule violations Engineer Review Beyond automated DRC, the layout is also reviewed from an engineering perspective. Depending on the project, this may include checking: Signal integrity Power integrity Thermal performance EMI/EMC considerations High-speed routing Manufacturing constraints Assembly requirements Mechanical compatibility Automated checks can identify rule violations, but they cannot replace engineering judgment. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. For PCB assembly projects, the BOM and pick-and-place files provide the component and placement information required for SMT assembly. Before release, the output files are checked to ensure that the generated manufacturing data is consistent with the approved PCB design. Step 8 – DFM and PCB Manufacturing The final stage is transferring the verified manufacturing data into production. Before fabrication, the manufacturing data can be evaluated against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities through Design for Manufacturability (DFM) checks. Typical DFM considerations include: Minimum trace width and spacing Minimum drill size Copper-to-edge clearance Annular ring requirements Solder mask clearance Via structures Board thickness Copper thickness Surface finish Manufacturing tolerances Manufacturing requirements are considered from the very beginning of PCBWay's PCB layout process, helping minimize production issues and unnecessary manufacturing delays. What’s more, upon completion of the PCB Layout order, free technical support and a permanent 5% discount on PCBA production will be provided. Why Professional PCB Layout Matters PCB layout has a direct impact on the performance and manufacturability of an electronic product. A professional PCB layout should consider the entire product development process—not just whether all components are electrically connected. Depending on the application, the layout may need to address: Signal Integrity (SI) Power Integrity (PI) EMI/EMC Thermal Management High-Speed Design Design for Manufacturability (DFM) Design for Assembly (DFA) Mechanical Integration Reliability and Serviceability The earlier these factors are considered, the fewer problems are likely to appear during prototype validation and mass production. Verify Now Blog > Remote-Sense Guidelines in Power Supply Design for DC-DC Converters Remote-Sense Guidelines in Power Supply Design for DC-DC Converters by: Mila Sep 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply design power module ir drop remote sens Many DC-DC power chips provide a Remote-Sense function. However, many designers mistake it for an optional secondary connection and wire it directly near the power module's local output. This setup effectively renders remote sampling useless. During the debugging phase, various anomalies may occur: while the local output voltage of the power module appears normal, the supply voltage at the BGA core experiences continuous droop; the power supply may exhibit audible noise, Loop Stability degradation, and severe output voltage ripple fluctuations. Remote-Sense is not a redundant line, but a Kelvin Sensing line used to measure the actual voltage at the load. The main power path carries high load currents, whereas the Force & Sense architecture ensures the Force & Sense signal paths remain isolated. Because the Force & Sense sensing line features high input impedance with minimal input bias current, it avoids the significant voltage drops present along the power delivery path, thereby measuring the load voltage more accurately. 1. Root Cause of Remote-Sense Application: DC IR Drop Modern processor core supply voltages continue to drop, with typical values around 0.8V or 0.85V, while operating currents can reach tens to hundreds of amperes. Even with wide copper traces and dense via arrays on the PCB, inherent DC resistance remains in the copper foil, connectors, vias, and BGA fanout regions along the power path. As large load currents pass through these impedances, a noticeable IR Drop occurs. For example, assume a DC-DC module has a local output voltage of 1.0V, and the total equivalent resistance of the power path from the module to an FPGA's BGA power pins is 1.5mΩ. Under a 100A load current, the voltage drop VIR Drop = I × R = 100A × 1.5mΩ = 150mV. Thus, while the local output stays at 1.0V, the actual voltage at the FPGA BGA pins drops to approximately 0.85V due to IR Drop along the copper, connectors, vias, and BGA fanout. If the sampling point is placed locally at the DC-DC output, the Feedback Loop can only detect the local 1.0V rail. The Feedback Loop remains unaware of the 0.15V lost before reaching the load. For low-voltage core supplies, the allowable voltage tolerance is tight, depending on processor, FPGA, or ASIC specifications. Such voltage degradation caused by IR Drop leads to full-load crashes, frequency throttling, and inadequate timing margins on high-speed interfaces. Remote-Sense resolves this problem: by routing the Remote-Sense sampling line directly near the load chip's power pins, the system detects the true voltage at the load. When the detected load voltage falls below the target, the Feedback Loop increases the power stage output to compensate for the IR Drop along the power delivery path. (Remote-Sense Working Principle) 2. Kelvin Remote Voltage Sensing: Force & Sense At its core, Remote-Sense relies on Kelvin Sensing principles to segregate the high-current power path from the voltage detection line. Force Power Path The power path delivers actual energy to the load and requires sufficient copper width, copper weight, and parallel vias to lower impedance. Because this pathway carries the full load current, it inevitably suffers from IR Drop. Sense Sampling Path The Force & Sense sensing line has high impedance and carries only a tiny input bias current. According to V = I × R, because the current flowing through the Force & Sense sensing line is negligible, its trace resistance creates virtually no voltage drop compared to the high-current power line. Consequently, Kelvin Sensing measures the electrical potential at the load with high accuracy. The power converter's internal Feedback Loop continuously measures the error between the sense voltage and an internal reference voltage, adjusting power delivery to compensate for PCB power losses. For ICs featuring Differential Sensing, both VSENSE+ and VSENSE- must be fully connected as specified in the datasheet. Incorrectly connecting only a single sense line may cause reference errors or disable remote sampling altogether. （Kelvin Force/Sense Schematic ） 3. Remote-Sense PCB Layout Guidelines Remote-Sense is far more than a simple jumper trace. Sampling point placement, routing methods, Noise Isolation, filtering, and Multi-Load Topology configurations all impose strict constraints. Improper implementation fails to compensate for IR Drop and risks introducing high-frequency noise into the Feedback Loop, inducing output fluctuations, degraded Loop Stability, or audible squealing. VSENSE+ / VSENSE- Differential Pair Routing VSENSE+ and VSENSE- must be routed using Differential Pair Routing, kept closely coupled in identical environments. Avoid placing either trace near SW Nodes, clock lines, or other noisy sources, and never run them parallel to power switching nodes over long distances. Adequate Noise Isolation is essential to prevent interference. If the two traces experience different distances to noise sources, varying Ground Plane Reference structures, or unequal surrounding copper, external interference couples unevenly into the lines. This asymmetry converts into differential-mode noise, directly corrupting the Feedback Loop. Therefore, the main objective of Differential Pair Routing is not simply maximizing line width, but ensuring both lines share a symmetrical, low-noise environment with effective Noise Isolation, minimal loop area, and a solid Ground Plane Reference. Sensing Point Placement Incorrect: Placing the Sensing Point Placement directly across the DC-DC module's local output capacitors. This neutralizes the benefits of Remote-Sense, as the controller senses only the local output while uncompensated losses persist down the line. Correct: Proper Sensing Point Placement requires connecting the lines as close as possible to the load chip's actual power pins (e.g., near the BGA power pins), adhering to the manufacturer's recommended Sensing Point Placement guidelines. Input filtering and Decoupling Capacitors must be placed as close to the chip power pins as possible to lower the high-frequency current loop impedance at the load. The core principle of Remote-Sense layout is: The sense point must represent the true voltage received by the load, not an intermediate node along the power path. Never place sense points arbitrarily along intermediate nodes or directly on power copper pour for layout convenience. Even if schematics correctly define Differential Sensing, improper Sensing Point Placement on the PCB invalidates the feature. （Remote-Sense PCB Layout） Controller-Side RC Low-Pass Filter Sense traces often traverse long PCB paths, making them vulnerable to high-frequency interference from switching SW Nodes, DDR buses, clocks, and high-speed traces. Proper Noise Isolation helps, but if high-frequency noise reaches the sensing node, it induces output jitter and degrades Loop Stability. For long sense traces or noisy environments, place an RC Low-Pass Filter near the sense pins according to datasheet recommendations to suppress coupled switching noise. Some IC manufacturers recommend an RC Low-Pass Filter consisting of tens of ohms in series and nanofarad-range capacitors. However, specific R and C parameters must strictly follow vendor datasheets and be validated through Loop Stability testing rather than using generic values. Note that an RC Low-Pass Filter introduces an additional time constant, requiring evaluation regarding its impact on loop bandwidth, Transient Response, and overall stability. Multi-Load Topology: Reference Point at Key Load When a single power rail supplies multiple BGA devices, a Multi-Load Topology must not place the sense point at a random common node or simply at the load closest to the converter. In a Multi-Load Topology, evaluate system voltage tolerances, load currents, and power path drops to position the reference point at the most voltage-sensitive load experiencing the highest drop. For example, in a chain of DC-DC -> Load A -> Load B -> Load C, if Load C has the tightest tolerance and highest line drop in this Multi-Load Topology, connect the sense reference point directly to Load C's supply pins. This ensures the loop prioritizes the voltage margin of the critical load, while closer loads are powered via the main power path without serving as feedback references. Handling Unused Remote-Sense Pins If a design does not enable Remote-Sense, do not leave the VSENSE+ and VSENSE- pins floating, as a Floating Pin Hazard will disrupt feedback control. For controllers relying on external sense inputs, a Floating Pin Hazard leaves input potentials uncontrolled, causing abnormal output voltages and potential device damage. To avoid a Floating Pin Hazard, consult the datasheet. Devices supporting local sense mode typically require connecting VSENSE+ to local VOUT+ and VSENSE- to local GND. Always follow the manufacturer's specified wiring for local sensing, as internal architectures vary. 4. Remote-Sense Cannot Replace Power Integrity / PDN Design Remote-Sense is not a substitute for proper load-side decoupling and low-impedance Power Integrity / PDN design. Remote-Sense primarily compensates for DC or low-frequency voltage losses along the power path. When a CPU, FPGA, GPU, or ASIC undergoes a fast step change, the Transient Response of the feedback loop cannot react instantaneously. During these events, Decoupling Capacitors and a low-impedance Power Integrity / PDN supply transient current and mitigate sharp voltage dips. Therefore, comprehensive Power Integrity / PDN design requires integrating multiple strategies: Low-impedance Power/GND planes with a continuous Ground Plane Reference Adequate copper width and parallel via arrays Load-side MLCC Decoupling Capacitors Bulk capacitors Optimized power routing Remote-Sense implementation High Transient Response and stable loop margins Remote-Sense, power path optimization, and Decoupling Capacitors complement each other rather than act as replacements. 5. Additional Remote-Sense Constraints and Safety Considerations If Remote-Sense is connected to a distant load without being properly configured or enabled, incorrect feedback compensation may drive the local voltage too high, triggering OVP / UVP Protection, instability, or exceeding maximum operating limits. Always consult the datasheet to confirm: Support for Remote-Sense and Differential Sensing Allowable voltage ranges for sense inputs Correct connections for local sensing mode Requirements for an RC Low-Pass Filter Optimal Sensing Point Placement Interaction between Remote-Sense and OVP / UVP Protection thresholds Maximum allowable sense trace lengths and routing layouts If the sense voltage drops excessively due to open circuits or extreme line losses, improperly configured controllers may trigger OVP / UVP Protection to prevent overvoltage damage at the local output or undervoltage failures at the load. Ultimately, Remote-Sense is not just about routing two lines to the load. It ensures the feedback loop accurately measures the actual voltage delivered to the load while maintaining reliable OVP / UVP Protection and preventing noise or parasitics from degrading system stability.l Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Why ICs Fail After Passing ESD Tests and How ESD Differs from EOS Why ICs Fail After Passing ESD Tests and How ESD Differs from EOS by: Mila Sep 14,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout ESD protection esd protection circuit Previous articles have covered key technologies related to chip ESD, including ESD diodes, power clamps, CDM mechanisms, and ESD testing procedures, with a focus on chip-level electrostatic discharge protection. However, a common problem in real-world engineering applications is that an IC may pass all standard ESD tests but still suffer damage or failure when used on an actual customer circuit board. Engineers often assume that the problem is insufficient chip-level ESD protection. However, this judgment has limitations. Not all electrical failures are caused by ESD. In many real-world applications, the underlying cause may instead be EOS (Electrical Overstress). 1. What Is EOS? EOS stands for Electrical Overstress. It refers to a condition in which an IC is subjected to voltage, current, or power stress beyond its designed safe operating limits, resulting in electrical abnormalities or physical damage. Common EOS Scenarios EOS can occur in many real-world application conditions, including: Power supply overvoltage I/O input voltage exceeding the specified limit Output short circuits Hot-plugging transients Line surge events Power supply reversal Negative voltage stress Ground bounce Abnormal power sequencing EOS is not a single standardized failure test model. Instead, it is a general term for failures caused by excessive electrical stress. Any voltage, current, or power stress that exceeds the device's designed tolerance can potentially result in EOS failure. 2. Key Differences Between EOS and ESD Both ESD and EOS can cause electrical damage to an IC, which is why they are easily confused in engineering practice. However, they differ significantly in terms of stress characteristics, duration, energy, and failure mechanisms. （Comparison of ESD and EOS Waveforms） 3. Why Can an IC Fail After Passing ESD Tests? Passing standardized HBM and CDM tests only demonstrates that an IC can withstand specific short-duration electrostatic discharge stresses under defined test conditions. It does not mean that the device can withstand every type of electrical transient that may occur in a real system. Standard ESD Tests Have Limited Coverage Standard ESD tests are designed around defined test models and conditions. They verify whether an IC's ESD protection structures and discharge paths can safely handle specified electrostatic pulses. However, these tests cannot reproduce every electrical stress that may occur after the IC is integrated into a complete circuit board. Real-World Applications Introduce Different Electrical Stress In actual circuit board applications, electrical stress may come from: Cable insertion and removal Power-on overshoot External load short circuits Surge coupling through long cables Back-EMF from motors, relays, and other inductive loads Transient ground potential rise Abnormal sequencing between multiple power domains Accidental power connection Compared with standardized ESD pulses, these events may have longer durations, higher accumulated energy, or repeated stress characteristics, resulting in different types of IC damage. The internal ESD protection circuit of an IC is primarily designed to handle short-duration electrostatic pulses. Its purpose is to establish a controlled discharge path and divert transient energy. Therefore, passing ESD tests does not mean that an IC has system-level protection against all EOS conditions. （ESD Test PASS vs Real PCB FAIL） 4. The Functional Limits of Internal ESD Protection A common misconception in system design is that an IC can withstand all external electrical disturbances simply because its pins include an ESD protection circuit. In practice, this assumption can create significant reliability risks. What Is Internal ESD Protection Designed For? The internal ESD protection structure is an important protection layer against electrostatic events. It is designed to provide a low-impedance path for short-duration ESD currents and prevent excessive voltage from reaching sensitive internal circuits. However, this protection is not intended to absorb large amounts of energy for an extended period. It should therefore not be treated as a substitute for system-level EOS protection. What Happens Under Sustained Overvoltage? For example, if an I/O pin is continuously exposed to a voltage beyond its specified operating range and the internal protection structure enters conduction, current may continue to flow into or through the IC. As the stress continues, the protection device and related circuits can generate significant heat. Depending on the electrical stress and internal current path, this may eventually cause damage to components such as: I/O protection devices Output driver circuits Power clamp structures Metal interconnects Vias PN junctions Core input circuits The actual damage location depends on the magnitude and duration of the external stress as well as the current path inside the IC. Why Board-Level Protection Is Required A key engineering principle is that internal ESD protection is primarily intended to handle short-duration electrostatic pulses, while system-level electrical stress with significant energy should be limited and protected at the board level. Common board-level protection methods include: TVS devices Series current-limiting resistors Power clamps Fuses Overcurrent protection Appropriate grounding Proper PCB layout The goal is not simply to add more protection components, but to limit the voltage, current, and energy that can reach the IC and provide a controlled path for transient energy. （Board-Level Protection + IC Internal ESD Protection） 5. Typical EOS Damage Locations and Failure Analysis EOS damage is closely related to the actual current path created by the electrical stress. Different types of stress can affect different areas of the IC: Power supply overvoltage: May damage power clamp structures, internal power circuits, metal interconnects, and thin gate-oxide devices. I/O input overvoltage: May damage I/O protection structures, input circuits, pull-up or pull-down protection structures, and core gate circuits. Output short circuit: May damage output driver circuits, metal interconnects, vias, and local diffusion regions. Negative voltage stress: May damage I/O protection structures, junction regions, and input/output circuits. Therefore, EOS failure analysis should not rely solely on the appearance of a localized burn mark. It is more important to trace the source of the electrical stress, current entry and exit paths, stress duration, and energy to identify the root cause. 6. Engineering Differences Between ESD and EOS Failure Signatures There is no absolute method for distinguishing ESD from EOS based solely on physical failure signatures. However, practical failure analysis often reveals some characteristic differences that can be used as initial clues. Common ESD failure characteristics include: Localized single-point damage Gate-oxide breakdown Abnormalities around I/O protection structures Localized PN-junction leakage Leakage or parameter changes at a single pin Common EOS failure characteristics include: More obvious thermal damage Localized melting or burning of metal Significant thermal damage to vias or metal interconnects Large-area circuit damage Abnormalities along power paths Damage to output driver circuits Simultaneous abnormalities across multiple pins or circuit nodes It is important to note that these failure signatures are only supporting evidence and should not be treated as final conclusions. Accurate differentiation between ESD and EOS failures requires comprehensive analysis of the failure scenario, electrical test data, application environment, test conditions, damage location, and physical analysis results. 7. The Risks of Misdiagnosing EOS as ESD In real-world applications, misdiagnosing an EOS failure as insufficient ESD protection can lead to an incorrect corrective strategy, wasting design resources while leaving the actual problem unresolved. When an IC is damaged by system-level EOS, simply increasing the size of the internal ESD protection structure, strengthening the internal power clamp, or widening internal metal interconnects generally cannot solve the system-level failure. The root cause may instead be related to board-level electrical stress, such as excessive external surge energy, improper TVS selection, continuous power supply overvoltage, load short circuits, abnormal hot-plug timing, or the lack of an appropriate freewheeling or clamping path for inductive loads. The key risk of misdiagnosing EOS is that engineers may continue to optimize the chip's ESD protection circuit without addressing the actual source and energy path of the system-level electrical stress. As a result, the same failure may occur repeatedly. Therefore, when investigating electrical failures in real-world applications, both chip-level and system-level factors should be considered rather than focusing only on the internal ESD structure. 8. Key Questions for Troubleshooting Suspected EOS Failures When an IC experiences an electrical failure, the following factors can be checked first to avoid automatically classifying the problem as an ESD failure: Failure Scenario Did the failure occur during a standard ESD test or during actual customer operation? Did it occur at the moment of power-up, during cable insertion or removal, after a load short circuit, or when a motor or relay was activated? Failure Location Is the problem limited to leakage at a single I/O pin, a low-resistance path between the power supply and ground, or simultaneous abnormalities across multiple pins? Has the overall operating current of the IC changed significantly? Stress Characteristics Was the failure caused by a short-duration transient pulse, continuous overvoltage, or overcurrent? Was there any periodic or repeated electrical stress or abnormal power sequencing? Board-Level Protection Does the circuit board include TVS or other surge protection? Is an appropriate current-limiting circuit provided? Does the power supply have overvoltage or clamping protection? Does the grounding path provide sufficiently low impedance? Does the inductive load have an appropriate freewheeling or clamping path? These factors can help determine whether the failure is related to system-level EOS and provide a basis for tracing the electrical stress path into the IC. Conclusion Both ESD and EOS can cause IC leakage, short circuits, functional abnormalities, and physical damage, but their stress characteristics, protection strategies, and corrective measures are significantly different. Passing standard ESD tests only verifies the IC's ability to withstand specific short-duration electrostatic pulses and does not cover every overvoltage, overcurrent, surge, hot-plugging, power reversal, or ground-bounce condition that may occur in a real system. Therefore, when investigating an IC failure in an actual application, engineers should not determine the root cause solely based on the fact that the device passed ESD testing or on the appearance of localized physical damage. Instead, the failure scenario, electrical stress, failure location, current path, board-level protection, and physical analysis results should be considered together. For electrical stress outside standard ESD test conditions, such as overvoltage, overcurrent, surge, hot-plugging, and inductive load transients, EOS should be considered as a potential root cause. Appropriate board-level protection can help limit the voltage, current, and energy reaching the IC and reduce the risk of application-level failure. Verify Now Blog > When vibration meets LoRa (and bandwidth fights back) When vibration meets LoRa (and bandwidth fights back) by: Engineer Sep 22,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in Technology Micropython Meshtastic Custom PCB Vibration sensor Summary： Using off the shelf hardware to measure vibration and transmit using LoRa. Here we are again. I’ve been working on a little clandestine project, I can’t fully name. Who is it for? The real application? What I can talk about is the tech. It’s a sensor project over a wireless protocol. Pretty standard for me. The short version: environment readings and vibration measurement using Meshtastic and LoRa. Completely enclosed local environment with web sockets, no cloud involvement at all. Before we get into the firmware wars, Let me tell you about what hardware I am using. The base platform I built the node around RAK Wireless WisBlock gear (ordered through Rokland): RAK4631 — Nordic nRF52840 BLE core + LoRa SX1262 RAK19007 — WisBlock Base Board 2nd Gen RAK1921 — WisBlock OLED display RAK1904 — 3-axis acceleration sensor For sensitivity tuning I needed an I²C rotary encoder. Adafruit’s STEMMA QT Rotary Encoder Breakout was one of the few low-cost I²C options that did exactly what I needed. Solid docs, worked flawlessly. A word of caution here, RAKWireless sells an I2C rotary encoder as well, but it is not compatible with the 3-axis sensor. I could get either one to work, but not both. I believe they must share an interrupt, that is my theory. I tried moving the 3-axis sensor to another slot, same problem. So, I went with the Adafruit rotary encoder instead. It has an added bonus of having a Neopixel mounted on the board which comes in handy later. Since the rotary encoder and OLED both use the I2C bus, I designed a small PCB to mount both and attach to the main board with JST connectors. (I hate JST connectors so much, I ended up just soldering wires from the boards because I just struggle with crimping the pins. Maybe someone smarter than this dumb hillbilly, with more patience, can tell me what I am doing wrong) Anyhoo.. Here is the board I designed to hold the OLED and the rotary encoder. The software (and the headaches) Architecture-wise, the node collects temperature, humidity, pressure, air quality, and vibration, then sends that data using Meshtastic over LoRa to a LoRa-to-Ethernet gateway that I built. Maybe another blog post on that one soon. The LoRa to Ethernet gateway forwards packets to a websocket on a NodeRed server. Sensor nodes stay mesh-connected so delivery stays reliable. Everything lives in one closed environment — nodes, collection, retention. Nothing over the internet. No cloud. 100% local and encrypted. Meshtastic’s built-in encryption is a nice bonus. Less time spent worrying about who might be listening in and really easy to configure. The problem Meshtastic is great but, there are limitations and they make perfect sense. The biggest one is bandwidth. LoRa means each node only gets to send a little data at a time. That’s fine for periodic temperature updates or a simple state change. Not so fine for data streaming. Everyone shares the airwaves. One chatty node can drown out the rest. For temp, humidity, pressure, and air quality, that’s easy, dial the transmit interval so everybody gets a turn. The standard environmental transmission interval is 15-30 minutes in the stock firmware. I changed that interval to 2 minutes in the firmware. This is a closed system; I only care what my nodes are saying. A note of caution though, if you make all the nodes talk a lot, you limit the number of nodes you can have on the mesh, in theory. Vibration is different. How do you capture vibration from multiple sources, get it across the mesh, and store it without chewing through all the bandwidth? The iterations I went through several versions. Some worked. Some taught me things the hard way. Attempt 1: The firehose. Stream live vibration data. One sensor was fine. Two sent too much data and consumed all the bandwidth, overloading the gateway. It listens for packets, then forwarded them serially to the web socket. I needed a faucet, not a firehose. Lesson one: don’t pour a lake through a straw. Attempt 2: Duty-cycled sampling. Stream for a few seconds, rest, stream, rest. Fine if you care about long-term trends. I wanted short-term anomalies too — What if i wanted to know if a truck was rolling past the house, or the dogs going full gladiator with a toy. Lesson two: selective data, not just less data. Attempt 3: Baseline + sensitivity. If the thing is already vibrating, what counts as an anomaly? You need a baseline. I set the firmware to wait 30 seconds after boot (so power-on bumps don’t poison the sample), then it collects ambient vibration for 30 seconds and builds a baseline. I used that baseline to compare any readings, used the rotary encoder to set sensitivity (how much above or below baseline is an actual anomaly?) and send 5 packets per anomaly with a 1ms wait between the packets. Below you can see the initial “bump”, then it goes back to almost normal for the remaining 4 packets. This should tell me if there are any resonant frequencies caused by the vibration over time. We will see though. More testing is needed here. The RAK1904 is a 3-axis accelerometer measuring force in G’s. Range and sample rate both matter when sampling. The sensor has several settings for how it measures force. After the usual loop of fail → fail → finally works, I landed on a 2g range setting (about 4 mg to trigger) and a high sample rate so quick spikes don’t get missed. (See my resonant frequency statement above) Slight variations still showed up in the baseline. At this point I was just reading X, Y, Z G-force though. I summed the three axes (X+Y+Z) and converted to an RMS-style reading (using 2 mm/s2), which gave me a baseline RMS with a peak. I also added a function where a single out of range sample doesn’t fire on a reading over peak, it wants two consecutive events which is more real world. A vibration doesn’t happen in one direction, see Newtons law. This sampling method is used so a random blip doesn’t spam the mesh. I could see this happening if the power was not clean so, wanted to assure that only real movement generated triggers. The firmware sends five consecutive readings using custom protobufs inside Meshtastic. I found that there are a bunch of unused protobufs set aside for “custom” work like this. So, I set the protobuf to 255. That way I can filter the data coming into the web socket (after decryption) by what protobuf it was using and that would tell me what was vibration data. Easy filtering into a NodeRed flow.. The rotary encoder adjusts sensitivity between about 0.5 and 15 mm/s², and the OLED shows the sensitivity setting you’re using/changing to. I setup the Neopixel to flash red on boot, until the baseline is complete. Once complete, the Neopixel changes to a solid green (armed, ready and sensing). When it is triggered, the Neopixel changes to a flashing blue. After it sends the data and the cooldown period, it changes back to green (armed) I have some real world testing to do, but I believe the sensor ready to be deployed. I am capturing data currently sending it to a local database and using Grafana to review the data. Here are some images of everything put together in a custom 3D printed enclosure. I used Fusion to design the enclosure and 3D printed in PLA for the prototype. If you want the firmware and related bits, they’re on GitHub: https://github.com/scottlecomte/rak-vibration-sensor Happy Making Makers! Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. AtomS3R AI Chatbot Kit Talking about the Composition of PCB Price Over the years, PCB price changes have been familiar with people inside and outside the industry, even though some people with years of experience in the PCB industry may not fully understand the ins and outs of this, so to analyze the main factors affecting pcb price: The diversity of prices caused by the different materials used in PCBs is based on common double-sided boards. Sheets generally include fr-4, cem-3, etc., and board thickness varies from 0.2mm to 5.0mm, and copper thickness varies from 0.5oz to 3oz. All of these have resulted in huge price differences on the sheet material; in solder mask inks, there are also certain price differences between ordinary thermoset oils and photosensitive green oils, and thus the diversity of materials has caused price diversity. The different production processes used by PCBs result in different production processes with different prices that will result in different costs. Such as gold-plated plates and sprayed tin plates, the production of the shape of the milling (milling) plate and beer (red) plate, the use of silk screen lines and dry film lines will have different costs, resulting in a variety of prices. The diversity of prices caused by the difficulty of the PCB itself Even if the material is the same, the process is the same, but the difficulty of the PCB itself will result in different costs. For example, if there are 1000 holes on both boards, the hole diameter of one board is more than 0.6mm and the hole diameter of the other board is less than 0.6mm, different drilling costs will be formed; if the two boards are the same, the linewidth is different. Differently, one type is larger than 0.2mm and one type is smaller than 0.2mm, which also causes different production costs, because the scrap rate of difficult plates is high, the inevitable cost is increased, and the price diversity is thus caused. Different customer requirements will also cause different prices The level of customer demand will directly affect the plate production rate, such as a board by ipc-a-600e, class1 requirements have a 98% pass rate, but according to class3 requirements may be only 90% The passing rate, resulting in different costs for the mill, eventually led to a change in the price of the product. The diversity of prices caused by different PCB manufacturers even if the same product, but because of different manufacturers of technology and equipment, different levels of technology, will also form a different cost, nowadays many manufacturers like to produce tin spray plate, because the process is simple, low cost, but Some manufacturers also produce gold-plated plates, resulting in higher scrap rates and higher costs. Therefore, they prefer to produce tin-spray plates, so their prices for tin-spray plates are lower than those for gold-plated plates. The price difference caused by different payment methods At present, PCB manufacturers generally adjust PCB prices according to different payment methods, ranging from 5% to 10%, which also results in price differences. Diversification of prices caused by regional differences At present, from the geographical point of view, prices have been increasing from south to north. There are certain differences in prices in different regions, and thus different regions have also caused price diversity. events.before: Resources / Blog / PA 12 - A High-Performance Material Perfect for Prototyping and Production PA 12 - A High-Performance Material Perfect for Prototyping and Production Written by Nathan Miller 4 min read Published January 27, 2022 Updated August 17, 2026 Learn more about PA 12, an incredibly versatile nylon polymer, and see how it can transform your next 3D printing project. Welcome to Xometry.com, your one-stop shop for all things 3D printing, CNC machining, sheet cutting, and injection molding! Whether you are looking for a way to kick-start your next prototyping project or ramp up to high-volume production , Xometry has you covered. We have access to dozens of high-performance materials that are the perfect match for your next 3D printing project. Today, we want to highlight an incredibly versatile material: Polyamide 12. What is a Polyamide, And Why Are There 12 of Them? Plastics have become a ubiquitous material found in products used throughout our modern life. What originally started as a way to replace pool balls made from elephant tusks (yes, that’s true). have become one of, if not the, most widely used materials for products around the world. One of the most useful kinds of plastics is nylon polymer. There are many different kinds of nylon polymers, and Polyamide 12 (PA 12), unsurprisingly, is a nylon polymer with 12 carbon atoms in it. This also explains its other commonly used name, nylon 12. Nylon polymers have many uses across a variety of industries. Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo So, what makes Polyamide 12 useful? Polyamide 12 is an ideal material if you are looking to 3D print complex and detailed parts because of its narrow melt window compared to other thermoplastics. This material can remain in an unmelted state and very quickly transition through melted and unmelted states through selective heating. Processes like selective laser sintering can create parts out of PA 12 by heating the nylon powder up to near melting, and with a touch of a laser create a controlled melt, fusing layers of parts together to make complex shapes. The printed material is strong, and its ability to endure stress gives it the flexibility to bend before it cracks, making it versatile for a number of high-stress applications. Polyamide 12 also has great chemical resistance, and it absorbs very little moisture. Combined with the enhanced design freedom inherent in 3D printing, PA 12 can be used for consumer goods, medical, industrial, aerospace, and other high-performance applications. What kind of end-uses does Polyamide 12 have? PA-12 is useful when safety, durability, and reliability are of critical importance. In the automotive industry , it's used all the time “In fuel lines, brake lines, pipelines — even the handles of certain power tools. PA 12 also is used in plastics for car seats and several consumer and sporting goods.” ( Source ). Polyamide 12 is also useful in the aerospace industry because it has great heat resistance. This is especially true for Polyamide 12 when it is combined with other additive and filler materials. Its chemical properties help make it resistant to abrasion, a useful characteristic when you are trying to design an aerospace part that won’t rip apart upon landing. In addition to PA 12, Xometry offers a wide range of temperature-resistant nylons with many different filler materials. PA 12 is also very useful in the medical industry for use in medical equipment because it is biocompatible and nontoxic. Biocompatibility refers to a plastic's ability “to act and perform without impairing basic immunological functions of the body. The use of biocompatible plastics in the medical field is aimed to enhance healing functions without causing injurious, negative physiological, allergic or toxic reactions.” ( Source ) PA 12 is incredibly useful plastic across many industries, but why should you use Xometry for Polyamide 12 end products? Xometry currently offers the ability to 3D print polyamide 12 across 3 manufacturing processes: HP Multi-Jet Fusion , Selective Laser Sintering , and Fused Deposition Molding . Each method has its own unique benefits, end-use applications, and relative costs. And if you are looking for other high-performance plastics, you’re in luck! Xometry has recently added four high-performance 3D printed plastics to its on-demand manufacturing services: Nylon 11 EX (Rilsan® Invent Natural), Nylon 12 CF (PA 602-CF), Nylon 12 AF (PA 605-A), and Nylon 12 HST (PA 620-MF). These highly durable plastics complement the already-available Nylon 12 and Nylon 12 Glass-filled (GB) materials at Xometry. All 3D printed nylons boast great feature resolution and a detailed surface finish, with the natural white powders available for color dyeing. With low costs, fast lead times, and the power of our global network behind us, we are equipped for your 3D printing orders, from rapid prototyping to high volume production . We encourage you to head over to the Xometry Instant Quoting Engine to get an instant quote for 3D printed parts in nylon 12 . And if you want to learn more about PA 12 and our other high-performance materials, check out our webinar: A Deep Dive into SLS 3D Printing and Our New High-Performance Materials . Very rewarding and highly recommended Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Very rewarding and highly recommended Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Very rewarding and highly recommended Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design. Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport.
